title: Aditi's milk vow
hook: a mother can't win back her sons' loss, so she keeps a vow
carry: a vrata puts in God's hands what you can't fix
tomorrow: the promised son is tiny. so what does he ask the king for?

segments.voice: Yesterday's last scene: a hand on a boy's head, and Prahlada's one wish spent on his father. The fierce god's hand is a blessing. Now the story moves on two generations, to Prahlada's grandson.

There's a particular helplessness in watching someone you love lose something you can't get back for them: a job, a place on a team, a home. In the Bhagavata Purana, that's Aditi. Her sons are the gods, and they've just lost heaven. Prahlada's grandson, Bali, a generous king of the asuras, has taken it, and the gods are in hiding. Aditi can't fight him. She can't fix it. So she sits at home, and grieves.
screen: `YOU CAN'T FIX IT FOR THEM.` → `HER SONS HAVE LOST HEAVEN.` → `SHE SITS, AND GRIEVES.`

segments.voice: Then her husband, the sage Kashyapa, comes home and finds the house gone quiet. He listens. He doesn't promise to fix it. Instead he gives her a vrata, a vow, to Vishnu: for the days of the vow she lives on milk and worships him each day. The text calls it payovrata, the milk vow. So Aditi keeps it, day after day. And at the end, Vishnu appears to her and promises: he'll be born as her son. When that son arrives, he's small, a young student who, in the telling, is given an umbrella and a water pot. His name is Vamana, the small one. Here's the teaching. Many teachers put it this way: a vrata isn't a bribe, and it isn't a fix. It's what a Hindu does when a thing is too big to carry: you take a vow, keep it steadily, and put what you can't fix in God's hands. Aditi's story is one of the old pictures of it, and the practice is still everywhere. Many Hindu mothers and grandmothers keep vratas for their children, a fast on a set day, a lamp, a prayer, often without telling anyone. And when help comes, it rarely comes the way anyone planned. Here, it comes small enough to hold.
screen: `HE LISTENS. HE DOESN'T FIX IT.` · `PAYOVRATA: THE MILK VOW.` · `A VRATA: PUT IT IN GOD'S HANDS.` · `STILL KEPT FOR CHILDREN TODAY.` · then, large: `SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: Think of one person carrying a loss you can't fix. Choose a tiny vow for them, small enough to keep: a lamp or candle each evening this week, a short prayer at bedtime, or, if you don't pray, one kind message each evening. Make the promise once, silently. Then give a few slow breaths to holding them in mind.
Vamana: Vishnu as the small one, a young dwarf student, born to Aditi after her steady vow.
Your line: a vrata puts in God's hands what you can't fix. Aditi kept hers, and Vamana came. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindus keep a vrata, a vow of fasting or simple worship over set days, for a family member in trouble; keeping the vow steadily is itself the offering.
